title: Comparing Internal Validation Methods for Clinical Risk Prediction
text: This simulation study compares three internal validation methods (sample splitting, cross-validation, and bootstrap) for clinical prediction models using 500 simulations with realistic sample sizes (n=858).

title: Comparing Internal Validation Methods for Clinical Risk Prediction
text:
3.1 Data Generating Process
Simulated scenario: - Binary outcome with 15% prevalence - 10 continuous predictors (X₁…X₁₀), all ~N(0,1) - Logistic regression with mixed effect sizes - Intercept (α = -1.9665) calculated to achieve exactly 15% prevalence
Model equation:
\[
\text{logit}(P(\text{outcome}=1)) = -1.9665 + 0.45X_1 + 0.40X_2 - 0.35X_3 + ... + 0.05X_{10}
\]

title: Comparing Internal Validation Methods for Clinical Risk Prediction
text:
3.2 Sample Sizes

Development: n=858 (129 events, EPV=12.9)

Determined using samplesizedev package

External validation: n=100,000
Simulations: 500 iterations

title: Comparing Internal Validation Methods for Clinical Risk Prediction
text:
3.3 Methods Compared
For each simulation:

Apparent validation - Optimistic test on development data (baseline)
Sample Split - 70/30 split
10-fold Cross-validation - Random folds; calibration slope is averaged across fold-wise slopes
Bootstrap - Harrell’s optimism correction (200 resamples)
External validation - Independent large dataset

title: Comparing Internal Validation Methods for Clinical Risk Prediction
text:
3.4 Performance Metrics

Discrimination: AUC (C-statistic). The true model has a C-statistic of 0.704.
Calibration: Calibration slope (1.0 = perfect; <1.0 = overfitting)
Overall accuracy: Brier score, Mean Absolute Prediction Error (MAPE)

External calibration slopes are computed using the same fitted models used for internal validation (bootstrap refits, CV fold models, and sample-split training models). For calibration slope, CV and bootstrap internal estimates are averaged across their fold/refit models to align with the external calculation. The earlier mismatch that compared refit-based internal slopes to a single full-model external slope is not used in this analysis.

4.4.4 Interpretation Note for Calibration Slope Correlations
The calibration-slope correlations are:

Sample split: 0.512
Cross-validation: -0.448
Bootstrap: -0.687

This sign pattern appears to be a property of the calibration-slope estimators used here rather than a coding error. Calibration slope is estimated from a second logistic regression (outcome ~ logit(prediction)), so it is more sensitive to sample-specific outcome noise than metrics like AUC, Brier score, or MAPE.
For CV and bootstrap, the internal slope is an average across many models fitted on development-derived data (fold complements or bootstrap resamples), while the matched external slope is averaged across those same models on an independent large dataset. Across simulations, development samples that induce stronger fitted coefficients tend to increase internal calibration slope but decrease external calibration slope, yielding an inverse between-simulation correlation. Sample splitting has much higher internal-slope noise (0.258 vs 0.062 for CV and 0.022 for bootstrap), which dilutes that inverse signal and can leave a net positive correlation.
Separate diagnostic scripts in this repository (debug_calibration_slope.R and test_hypothesis.R) reproduce the negative CV/bootstrap correlation and support this interpretation.

title: Comparing Internal Validation Methods for Clinical Risk Prediction
text:
5.1 Methods
For each of 1000 simulations:

Generate training data (n=858, following Pavlou’s sample size recommendation)
Fit a logistic regression model on the training data
Validate the model on external datasets of varying sizes:

n = 858, 1716, 3432, 6864, 13728, 27456, 54912, 1e+05

Calculate performance metrics (AUC, calibration slope, Brier score, MAPE) for each validation size

This design isolates the effect of validation sample size on performance estimate variability and correlation with the asymptotic ‘truth’ (n=100,000).

title: Comparing Internal Validation Methods for Clinical Risk Prediction
text:
5.4 External Validation Results
Calibration slope and MAPE achieve correlation = 0.9 somewhere between 4x and 6x the training size, while AUC requires 12x to achieve 83.5%. Brier Score never exceeds 0.5 correlation, even at 12x. Calibration, AUC and MAPE yield substantial improvements in variability with increasing validation sizes, while the Brier Score’s variability hardly changes. Across the board, the marginal gain in precision diminishes substantially beyond ~10× the training size.
